subtopic: IMPORTATION OF CELERY FROM THE UNITED STATES
IMPORTATION OF CELERY FROM THE UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: PETITION FOR EMBARGO FROM LAMBTON COUNTY GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to present a petition from the celery growers in my constituency which reads as follows:
To the honourable the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembied
The petition of the undersigned celery growers of the constituency of East Lambton, Ontario, humbly showeth: That we desire to have an embargo piaced on celery coming from the United States into Canada similar to the embargo placed on this product going into the United States from Canada by the government of the United States, from October to February of each year.
Wherefore your petitioners humbly pray that your honourable House may be pleased to grant the prayer of this petition, and as in duty bound your petitioners will ever pray. May 18th 1926.
The explanatory note is very short. It reads as follows:
Thedford, Ont., May 18, 1926.
J. E. Armstrong, Esq.,
Member of House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
Enclosed find two copies ol our petition for the Senate and the House of Commons.
For your information the duty on celery entering the United States is twenty-five per cent and an embargo has been on for years against the celery from

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
Canada entering the United States on account of the com borer which to date has never bothered celery but is used as a handle to stop exportation.
We would appreciate it as a body if an embargo was on from October to February 1st each year, so as to allow the local supply to be consumed before the southern states flood the market.
This resquast is asked not as a handle to boost prices but to allow the home grown product to have the market and work off the supply before foreign goods come on.
Thanking you in advance and trusting you will be successful in our cause,
I remain,
Yours very sincerely,
Chas. Kinmerley.
I may say that the crop grown in the district in 1924 consisted of over 250 carloads.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT EMPLOYMENT OFFICE ADVERTISING FOR MEN
speechtext: I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the information I have received is to the effect that applications were made for workers by some of the mines in Nova Scotia. The applications were communicated to the department which asked its various agencies for information as to the extent to which these demands could be supplied. The reply received was to the effect that there were, perhaps, sufficient workers available in Canada to meet the requirements. Up to the present it has not been deemed necessary or advisable to at all comply with the request which was made for additional workers from outside Canada. That is the information on the matter so far as I have been able to obtain it.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee of Supply.
He said':	In attempting to present, for the
consideration of parliament, what has come to be known as the railway budget, I do so with every appreciation of my own somewhat recent contact with federal railway affairs. Since taking hold, I have gone far enough into the activities of the department over which I have the honour to preside to acquire a lively appreciation also of the splendid service rendered by that veteran of public life and my own immediate predecessor, the Right Hon. George P. Graham. We on this side of the House regret his absence to-day and none more so than the one to whom has fallen the difficult task which years of experience had made so easy for the former minister. Mr. Graham had the very happy faculty of presenting National railway matters in such a way as to invite their consideration on a high plane. It is my wish that there should be no departure from that very desirable practice, and that whatever criticism there may be-and criticism there is bound to be- may be of a constructive and helpful nature, and to the advantage rather than hurt of the country's immense investment in our National railways.
Following the precedent established last year the Canadian National railway report was this year made available in advance of the minister's annual statement, and has been in the hands of the members for some weeks. The report presents much detail, not only as to operating results, but of the financial ramifications of the system. It is well that such full information as to the management and operation of the National lines should be freely available to parliament. The National railways are the people's property, in the success of which the Canadian public are deeply concerned, and, as representatives of the owners, it is desirable that members of this House should take a very close interest in our railway affairs.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
Last year's operating results were so far in in advance of previous years that I feel that my first duty in relation to the report itself should be the altogether happy one of congratulating the chairman and president, the board, the responsible officers and the rank and file of the National railways on the results achieved. To have done more business at less cost is an accomplishment which has brought commendation from quarters ordinarily inclined to hold that such things were not really possible under public ownership. The figures indicate roughly that while two-thirds of this year's improvement of fifteen millions in net earnings was the result of increased business due to a good harvest and improving trade, one-third was due to decreased costs of operation. And it will be noted that Sir Henry Thornton affirms that this improvement was accompanied by no deterioration in service or unfair treatment of employees. It affords me pleasure, therefore, on behalf of the government, to acknowledge the loyal service of officers and employees, whose enthusiasm and good will made last year's achievement possible.
This gathering, Mr. Speaker, in the House of Commons, is the only body which bears the relationship to our National Railways which is borne by the annual shareholders meetings of a private company to the affairs of that company, and I propose to deal with the subject this afternoon rather as if the members of this House were, as they are, representatives of the great body. of shareholders throughout the Dominion of Canada in this property. The presentation I will endeavour to make will be analytical in character rather from the point of view of a man who comes freshly into contact with the railway system and its affairs, and who settles down to study the system, and probably my point of view will be more interesting because of that.
The accounts are presented in balance sheet form as designed by the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States, and adopted by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. The form is that used by the railroads of the United States, and by the use of such a standard form, comparison is readily made with the accounts of other railroads which have adopted this standard of accounting practice. The balance sheet of the National lines carries the signature of the chief accounting officer of the railways and, in addition, the certificate of a well-known firm of chartered accountants.
It should be kept in mind that this is not the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railway Company, but is a consolidated
balance sheet designed to show the aggregate assets and liabilities, under each balance sheet classification, of every company embraced within the Canadian National system, with all inter-corporate transactions eliminated. By this form of presentation there is clearly displayed the total assets under the control of the National Railways, the total liabilities to the public against such assets, and the total liabilities for capital less deficits to the government as shareholders, and for loans and advances.
The Central Vermont Railway is not included in this consolidation except in respect of the control account with that company carried in the National books under investments in affiliated companies. It will be of interest to honourable members to know that there are no less than 87 separate balance sheets included in this consolidated account. Between many of these individual balance sheets are numerous inter-related transactions which require to be eliminated in any consolidation so as to present a clear picture of the relationship of the National Railways to its public creditors and to the government.
I believe every hon. member has in his desk a copy of the annual report, and will be able to follow my reference to the various pages of that report.
On the asset side of the balance sheet it will be seen that the accounts are separated under four headings-Investments, Current Assets, Deferred Assets, and Unadjusted Debits-and that on the liability side, a corresponding separation is made. A classification under Interstate Commerce Commission standard headings of expenditures, less retirements, during the year 1925, applicable to investment in road and equipment, is given on page 23 of the report, and similar information relating to improvements on leased railway property will be found on page 24. These statements indicate a net improvement of $17,964,827 during the year in the railways' investment in road and equipment, and of $430,628 on leased railway properties.
In the next item, sinking funds which have been created in accordance with the provisions of trust deeds for the redemption of certain items of funded debt, there is a balance of $9,374,000 of which $5,064,000 represents the par of system securities acquired, but held alive in such sinking funds. This should be considered in the sense of a reduction to that extent of the total funded debt held by the public.
The item, miscellaneous physical property, $53,912,609, includes hotels, lands, and so on, and in connection with the latter a footnote directs attention to the fact that the provinces

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
of Ontario and Quebec dispute the title of lands valued at $7,318,140.
A detail of the investment in affiliated companies is given on page 37 of the report. In this list is a new account of $3,677,500, representing acquired bonds of the Toronto Terminal Railway Company issued in connection with the financing of the Toronto new station and viaduct scheme in connection with which legislation was enacted last session. Twenty-five millions odd of this thirty-seven millions shown as investments in affiliated companies represent the Canadian National holdings in the Central Vermont.
The next group of accounts, Current Assets, shows a total of $95,500,000 as against $99,-
500,000	last year. Cash on hand in the general funds of the company which, at December 31, last, totalled $31,677,083, is up $1,669,000. Special deposits, which represent funds set aside for specific purposes, are up $4,000,000. In thig account are carried unexpended balances of proceeds of securities which are released, from time to time, on the authority of the Minister of Finance. Miscellaneous accounts receivable are down $2,500,000. Part of this decrease is due to accounting reclassification, but the decrease is also attributable to better collections, indicating better business conditions generally. The value of materials and supplies on hand at December 31, was $42,582,983, as compared with $50,459,444 at the end of the previous year. As explained by Sir Henry Thornton in his review of the year's operations, expenditures on purchasing and stores account were considerably less in 1925 than in 1924. A determined effort also was made to reduce stocks, so that at the end of the year, materials and supplies on hand amounted to almost eight millions less than at the end of 1924.
Under Deferred Assets-Insurance and Other Funds-is carried the investment of the company's fire insurance and other reserve funds which I will refer to when I come to the reserves under deferred liabilities. The increase of a million in other deferred assets is occasioned by accounting reclassification.
Discount on funded debt, an unadjusted debit item, represents the discount below par at the time of the sale of all securities, which discount is amortized by charges to income account in equal amounts over the life of the securities.
On the other side of the balance sheet the principal account is that of long-term debt, which shows an increase during the year of $63,630,126.52. It will be noted that in this year's presentation it is made a little clearer that this account includes interest accrued on government loans, which, under present

conditions, is a matter of book-keeping only and does not represent additional cash advances by the government. This interest account has been increased by $31,703,510.70 during the year, and now accumulates to more than $161,000,000. Analyzing the increase in debt of $63,000,000 during the year, we shall find the debt held by the public has increased $17,416,219.94, and the debt to the government $46,213,906.58. The increase in the debt to the public, as explained under the heading of Finance on page 6 of the report, comprises two guaranteed issues, one of $17,000,000, and the other $18,000,000, against which there were retirements amounting to $17,583,780.06. The increase in debt to the government of $46,213,906.58 is made up of three items, the first of which is the book-keeping item of interest accrued on government loans, $31,703,510.70. It will be well to keep in mind, in discussing the railway debt, that a large portion of the increase in debt as shown by the railway accounts is not additional cash advanced by the government to the road, but is this item of interest which they are compelled to set up in their books. I wish to emphasize this because frequently the impression gets abroad that the railway has used up during the year much more cash than is actually the case. For the year 1925, for instance, of the increase in debt, approximately one-half is cash and the rest is a bookkeeping transaction.
The second item in the increase in government debt is an amount of $14,259,435.69 repaid to the railway. When the railway issued its four and a half per cent gold bonds in September, 1924, the proceeds not immediately required were temporarily lent to the Minister of Finance and were repaid by the minister to the railways in the early part of 1925. The third item is an amount of $250,960.19 representing certain payments made through the Department of Railways and Canals for compensation and pension payments to Canadian Government railway employees under special legislation, which are taken up in the accounts of the National Railways so as to make a complete accounting for the entire property.
Full details of the outstanding debt held by the public, or by sinking funds, are to be found on pages 28 and 29 of the report. The schedule also shows to what extent the outstanding securities are guaranteed by Canada or the provinces, and indicates that, of the $931,000,000 of funded debt due the public, $674,000,000 is guaranteed and $256,000,000 is unguaranteed. Of the $674,000,000 guaranteed, $581,000,000 is guaranteed by the Dominion and $93,000,000 by the various

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
provinces, as follows:	Ontario, $7,859,997;
Manitoba, $24,389,892; Saskatchewan, $17904,061; Alberta, $18,394,427, and British Columbia, $25,026,001. Grand Trunk debentures of 216 millions, included in the guarantees by the Dominion, are guaranteed as to interest only under the Grand Trunk Railway acquisition agreement.
The provincial guarantees have, in effect, been taken over by the Dominion, since it has also acquired the properties. There never was any question of interest being paid other than by the Dominion so far as any of the Canadian Northern guarantees are concerned. In the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific, complications due to receivership created confusion at first and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were obliged to meet certain branch line interest payments. It developed that on the provinces meeting this obligation over four six-monthly interest periods, they could have taken possession of the Grand Trunk Pacific branch line properties. Former President Hanna, considering that these branches would be useful to the National system, recommended that they bs retained by the Dominion. The danger of partition of this Grand Trunk Pacific property was thus avoided, the two provinces concerned were reimbursed the interest charges they had met, and the Dominion has since provided the interest.
In the debt due the government is included appropriations account of the Canadian Government Railways amounting to $453,935,303. As is well known, this item includes the direct contributions by the Dominion to the Intercolonial and branch lines, the Prince Edward Island railway in Eastern Canada, the Transcontinental railway between Moncton and Winnipeg, including the Quebec bridge, and also the construction cost of the Hudson Bay railway. It also includes the working capital advanced from year to year by the government to those railways prior to their being taken over by the Canadian National for management and operation, and
it also includes the operating losses cn those railways since January 1, 1921, at which date authority was taken to pay operating expenses out of earnings. It is understood, of course, that this item of $453,935,303 is not a liability of the Canadian National Railway Company, but is brought into the consolidated balance sheet as the offset account against the assets of the Canadian Government railways as set up at their ledger value.
It will be observed that the total of loans and advances on Dominion of Canada account is shown in the balance sheet as 572 millions. Hon. gentlemen may have noticed that the Minister of Finance, in his budget speech, stated that the actual cash outlay in respect of these railway corporations charged to the debt of the Dominion, was 601 millions. The apparent discrepancy of $28720,547 is accounted for by these circumstances:	The ten millions advanced by the
government to the railways was made after December 31 last, and appears in the budget statement, but not in the railway statement. The railway does not include in loans and advances $8,720,547.06 voted under Advances to Canadian National Railways and utilized for requirements of Canadian government railways. The amount is added by the railways to the separately-shown Appropriations account, Canadian Government Railways. The balance of the difference is the ten million dollars paid by the Dominion for Canadian Northern commoa stock. Naturally, that item has no place in the railways' loan account with the Dominion.
I have here a statement showing the allocation of these 601 millions to March 31 last. It is of interest in that it shows the extent to which these government loans and ad- ' vances have gone to meet operating deficits, interest, refunding and retirements, capital expenditure and to working capital. With the permission of the House, I would like to hand the statement to Hansard, for the information of the members generally.

Turning now to some of the other items on the liability side of the balance sheet, traffic balances and accounts payable show an increase due to additional business at the close of the year. Interest matured, unpaid, shows a substantial reduction of $6,500,000, due principally to a reclassification of unpaid interest on the Grand Trunk Pacific 4 per cent debenture stock. The interest on this security is accrued by charge against income, but is not paid if not earned. Unpaid arrears

are now classified as a deferred liability, and this explains the increase in the item, Other Deferred Liabilities.
Under unadjusted credits, insurance and casualty reserves increased $1,408,000 of which $1,387,000 is the fire insurance reserve. The merchant marine is also insured through the railway insurance fund. The steady increase in this reserve indicates the wisdom of the policy adopted in placing insurance

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
through the company's own fund instead of outside underwriters. Under present policy, all profits which the underwriters would have received, remain with the company.
Profit and Loss account, being a debit balance, is shown as an impairment of the government equity in the property as represented by $265,628,338.70 of capital stock owned by the Dominion and $1,188,482,341.48 in Dominion of Canada account.
Before leaving the balance sheet, I would just like to make one further observation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in his budget speech, estimated that for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1926, there was a shortage of net earnings against the interest payable to the public of $7,400,000. When the budget speech was delivered, the actual figures for the government fiscal year were not available. Since they have been available, it is shown that the position is even better, and that the deficiency in net earnings to meet interest charges due the public was not $7,400,000, but $5,735,502-and this after allowing for such charges as amortization of discount, depreciation accruals, and retirements of the ledger value of equipment taken out of service, amounting in all to more than three million dollars.

It is now six years since the government became responsible for Grand Trunk financing, and while the reorganization and consolidation of the National system did not take place until late in 1922, we have a six-year background from which to judge of the progress made by the railways towards recovery from the difficulties which proved too much for private ownership. There are a number of ways in which progress may be noted. It is four years now since there has been an operating deficit. In 1920 the operating deficit was $34,GO0,0O0. In 1925 there was an operating surplus of $32,000,000. The extreme swing between the operating deficit of 1920 and the operating surplus of 1925 was $66,000,000, or an average improvement, over that period, of 11 millions a year.
A very hopeful feature also of our railway situation is the fact that the annual increase in operating earnings in recent years has been greatly in excess of the annual increase in fixed charges. While as stated, the total of the annual increases in operating earnings during the last six years was 66 millions, the total of the annual increases in fixed charges over that period was but 26 millions, or 40 millions less.
There has been improvement, also, in the matter of total deficit, including fixed charges. Six years ago, it was $80,000,000, while. last year it was $41,000,000-or about one-half. And of this deficit of 41 millions for 1925, 31 millions was a book-keeping charge for unpaid interest due the government, which has been written into the debt of the railway.
During the six years in question, the debt of the railway due the public increased by 130 millions, and the debt due the government-including interest-by 506 millions-a total of 636 millions. But of the latter sum 153 millions consisted of government interest. It may be asked why this item of interest should be segregated. Such a question might

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
be answered in this fashion, if applied to an ordinary case of loan on mortgage. The mortgagor failed, and the chief creditor took over the property on his own account, and that of other creditors interested. But the requirements of present railway accounting methods make it necessary to continue to set up the interest charges, although the government, the chief creditor, has taken over the property. Such a situation could rarely arise in an ordinary business transaction.
There has been criticism, in another place, to the effect that there is no assurance that the increase in railway debt would grow less in the near future. The answer is that the annual increase already grows smaller. Including government interest, the increase in railway debt has, as stated, amounted to 636 millions during the last six years. Stripped of the 153 millions of government interest the increase was 483 millions. Of the 483 millions, 243 millions were added during the two years 1920 and 1921, and 239 millions during the succeeding four years. In 1920, the actual addition to the debt, omitting the bookkeeping charge of government interests, was 131 millions; in 1925 it was $31,926,617. Quite clearly then, there is substantial reduction in the rate of increase in the railway debt.
I have pointed out that the debt of the railway increased to a greater extent during 1920 and 1921 than in the four years since. There were reasons for that, and in fairness to those responsible during those years, I should state that the railways, during 1920 and 1921, were at the very depth of their difficulties. It so happened that heavy maturities coincided with the peak of the deficits, and there were as well consistently heavy demands on capital account. Thus the total requirements of the railways were heavier in those years than they have, ever been since that time or are ever likely to be again. The bulk of the burden of financing the railways fell upon the government, private capital at that time not being entirely sure of the National Railway situation, and there was the added fact that money was not as plentiful as it has since become. That condition may be traced in the statement of the railway's unmatured funded debt, and will be found expressed in rates of interest which, even with the guarantee of the government, ranged as high as 7 per cent, in contrast with the 4 and 4i per cent issues put out in 1924 and 1925.
I now come to what seems to be a contentious matter in this chamber, the question of assistance to the railways in the form of guarantee rather than by direct aid, and, as a newcomer to the federal arena, I have endeavoured to

familiarize myself with the actual situation, not with the object of provoking further controversy, but with a view to ascertaining in what particular, if any, there has been change of practice and policy.
I find that prior to 1921-22, issues guaranteed were additional to the cash vote, as certain subsequent issues have been. In that way, the guarantees of 1920-21 were for refunding, and could not be utilized for any other purpose.
In 1921-22 for the first time, the estimates provided that advances to the railways might be made in the form of cash, or by way of guarantee, or partly in cash and partly by guarantee, in the discretion of the Governor-in-Council. It was further provided that the moneys thus loaned could be used on any of the following accounts, (a) operating deficits,
(b)	acquisition of "property, materials and supplies, (c) interest on notes, securities or Obligations, (d) the principal or interest on maturing or matured loans, secured or unsecured, and (e) construction and betterments. Thus it was specifically provided that the guarantees of that year, which of course reduced the cash vote to that extent, could be used for general purposes, and the 50 millions guaranteed that year were so utilized. The general form of this estimate has simply been continued by the present government. There is nothing wrong about it, and the utilization of such moneys is of record in both railway and departmental reports. Unquestionably, the moneys were utilized by the railways in accordance with the provision of the vote. Had they not been, the auditors whose duty it is to watch such matters would have had something to say. The practice, therefore, has been consistent since the present form of vote was introduced in 1921-22.

Does the hon. member not
*think it is fair to say that the Canadian National Railway consists to a fairly great degree of what are known and described by the minister as colonization lines. Those lines cost a good deal more to operate than the Canadian Pacific lines which were built more as business lines. The Canadian National Railway consists of a number of systems not built for business, but which must be operated as part of the system.

My point is that if it ,can be shown that the gross earnings on the mileage of the Canadian National railway is less than the earnings on the Canadian Pacific railway, the argument holds good. But if the gross earnings per mile of the Canadian National railway were equal to the gross earnings of the Canadian Pacific railway, then what one gains in one place is offset by what the other gains in another place.
Gross earnings per mile?

Yes, you will find that in 1924 the gross earnings per mile on the Canadian National were higher than on the (Canadian Pacific railway. In 1925 the gross earnings per mile were practically the same, (but the difference in operating cost on maintenance of way was the difference between $1,698 and $2,050. In transportation cost the Canadian National could save 81 per cent and in maintenance of equipment 1.7 per cent.
I am not going into details, but anyone who desires to get the information for himself can obtain it by referring to the operating statement of the Canadian National Railways for 1925 in which year the showing was better than usual, but what do you find? You find that it was in some degree due to the fact that they allowed their equipment to run down, *because they had less rolling stock in service at the end of 1925 than at the end of 1924,

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
.indicating that a considerable part of their rolling stock was out of repair and could not ibe used.
In connection with the matter of proper freight charges, my hon. friend referred to the much debated point as to whether we were handling traffic in some parts of the country at less than cost. The fact that the railways earn more money in the last three months of the year than in the first, second or third three-month periods, indicates, it is claimed, that the major part of traffic they handle during the last three months is the most profitable kind of traffic they have. Turn to the operating expenses, and hon. members will find that for maintenance of equipment the Canadian National Railways spent $47,902,092.16 and for maintenance of way $43,006,813.70, a total under these two items alone in round figures of $90,000,000 spent for maintenance of way and maintenance of equipment. When is that money spent? In the first place, there is a heavy traffic on all lines in Canada in the last four or five months of the year, commercial as well as grain traffic-very much greater than in the first half of the year. The equipment begins to be retired at a very early period in the new year, and sent to the repair shops to be put into condition for the fall operations and at least 75 per cent of the $47,000,000 for the maintenance of equipment is spent in the first half of the year.
Anyone who knows anything about maintenance of way costs on a railway knows that those costs take place in March, April, May, June, July and the first half of August. Maintenance of way costs are reduced to a minimum beginning with the middle of August or the first of September. I am making this statement simply in order to show how easy it is by taking group figures to reach a fallacious conclusion in relation to the operation of these railways. Approximately 30,000 cars must be gathered in western Canada to move the grain crop and these cars are sent west commencing with the first of the year. On either the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National you will find to-day long strings of empty equipment being sent to the west. The operating charges for moving this empty equipment to western Canada are applicable to the day the equipment is moved. Those empty cars are set out on side tracks and they remain idle for the time being. Another point in connection with the movement of this seasonal traffic is that those 30,000 cars are used almost exclusively for the movement of the grain crop. This situation is not peculiar to Canada; the same thing is true in the United States, both in the west in connection

with the grain crop and in the south in connection with the cotton crop. The crops must be moved when they are ready to be moved, so that the railways must have a large quantity of rolling stock which they otherwise would not require. On the Canadian railways at least 30,000 freight cars could be abandoned altogether if the total freight movement was distributed equally over the twelve months of the year. Those 30,000 freight cars mean an investment of $90,000,000 and the capital charges must be kept up in addition to the equipment being maintained in proper condition. I refer to that, not from a controversial standpoint, because transportation is the question before the Canadian people to-day that must be solved if we are going to get down to a sound industrial and economic basis. There are in my opinion commodities both east and west that must be moved at a minimum of cost. We must find a means of moving the surplus grain crop out of western Canada and the coal and iron of the east to central Canada at a minimum of cost.
What does the hon. gentleman mean when he speaks about a minimum of cost? Would he base his rates on cost, or less than cost, or more than cost?

That is a question
that must be determined, but I will answer my hon. friend in this way. I am not averse to saying that in order to develop western Canada by assisting in the movement of the surplus grain crop to the markets of the world, and particularly through Canadian ports, it might be, and I believe would be, a wise policy for Canada to carry that grain crop at less than cost if necessary.	-

Would the hon. member
bring that policy into effect by a reduction of rates or by means of a subsidy?

I will come to that,
if my hon. friend will allow me. In order to develop industry in eastern Canada, particularly in relation to coal and steel, I believe it would be wise for the Canadian people to consider moving that traffic for less than cost. How are we going to make up the difference? There are only two ways in which this may be done. One is by direct cash subvention, and I do not believe that is necessary or wise, because in the first instance it would be a difficult matter to determine what the cash subvention should be. The other way is to distribute the reduced cost of handling the traffic of the far west and the traffic of the east over the other classes of traffic that are handled in the more densely populated parts of Canada. How can we accomplish that?

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
There is just one way in which it can be done, and this is a point that is being entirely lost sight of. We should first establish an equitable rate structure for all commodities for all parts of Canada. I understand that the matter has been referred to the Board of Railway Commissioners. While they have the matter before them, what do we find? We find that special commodities are being taken and special rates . applied, making it utterly impossible for the Board of Railway Commissioners, I care not how expert they may be, to establish an equitable rate structure in this country. We must first start with the Canadian National Railways and determine the capital cost that should be applied to it. Then we must put in charge men who will operate it so that it will earn enough money to pay operating expenses and interest on capital costs. We have not made a start at doing that yet. After that is accomplished we must ask the Board of Railway Commissioners to establish what will be equitable rates.
Another reason why equitable rates cannot be established at the present time is because of the unfair competition that exists owing to the fact that the Canadian National Railways are not called upon to earn the money necessary to operate them. So long as that condition exists neither the Canadian National nor its competitor can reach a point where it can stand the application of an equitable rate. To put it in plain terms, so long as the Canadian Pacific is subjected to the form of competition that can be applied against it by a system of railways that is not called upon to earn its operating costs and to pay a return on the money invested in it, the Canadian Pacific cannot bear the application of an equitable rate structure. That is the point.	.
In that regard may I say one further word and I will conclude? We have heard a great deal in the last two or three years with regard to getting- rid of duplicate services; it is said that the two railways should get together; that unnecessary trains should be taken off here and there. We must start first with the Canadian National Railways itself:	let us
begin by eliminating some of the duplicate lines. If we eliminate 1,000 miles of unnecessary lines of the main line of the Canadian National Railways we shall save on the item of maintenance of way and transportation alone $5,000,000 a year. In addition we shall get all the material on these lines to build branch lines in western Canada. Can anyone tell the House or the country why the Canadian National Railways should have two lines of railway starting at the city of
Montreal and paralleling each other from there to the town of Sudbury, running side by side and competing with each other for business? Just a short time ago I went with a member of this House to an Ontario town on the Canadian National Railways. I went to the Canadian National ticket office to make a reservation and I made a reservation to go out on a night train. The man who brought me to the station took me to another station entirely. I said:	"You must be
making a mistake; this must be the Canadian Pacific." He said: "No, this is another Canadian National system." It was a beautiful station, all lit up with electric lights, with a ticket agent, telegraph operator, baggage express man, and so on, but it was not the station at which this train came in at two o'clock in the morning. I said: "Do you mean to tell me that the Canadian National Railway has two stations in this town each competing with the other for business?" He sand: "Why, certainly. One is the Canadian Northern station and the other is the Grand Trunk station." This was on the Grand Trunk double track line, the best piece of railway in the country, with the Canadian Northern line competing with it. The same thing is occurring all over the country.
No. .
What about the stretch between Winnipeg and Brandon?
Those lines serve local purposes.
That is the point.

They serve local purposes, my hon. friend says. When two trains leave the terminal at Winnipeg side by side and you stand on the observation platform of one, how much of the line is there from which you cannot see the other train? You would see mile upon mile the other railway track running almost parallel. As a matter of fact, for miles they are within a hundred yards of each other.
No.
I beg your pardon; it is so between Winnipeg and Portage la Prairie.
Both lines run into Portage la Prairie.

Yes, and the only
trouble is that the two lines cannot be used as a double track. If the rails of the one were taken up and laid alongside the other, so that the two might be used as a double track, some purpose would be accomplished,

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
but as it is now there is a duplication of service along the main lines. However, I will not labour that point. It is certainly most unfortunate that there should be such keen competition for business in the various towns in which one sees two ticket offices vieing with each other for public business. The policy is absolutely unsound and the first thing for us to do if we are to make any progress in the direction of solving our railway problem is to eliminate this unwarrantable duplication of service.
The minister has referred to the construction of branch lines. So long as Canada continues to develop we shall need to build branch lines to meet the demands of that development, but our first aim should be to reduce to the very minimum the duplication which at present is so costly to our transportation system. The minister also expressed the opinion that the solution for our railway problem is to be found in an increase in population. I agree with him. And, let me add, the solution for that problem is, in turn, the inauguration of a sound industrial policy in this country, a policy which will render such an increase in population possible.

Another Daniel has come to judgment, for the hon. member (Mr. Nicholson) now confesses that there is an altogether unnecessary duplication of railway service in this country. As one lone individual in parliament, and outside as well, I have been emphasizing this fact for years,_ and now I am glad to see that in all quarters it is receiving increasing recognition. This morning I read in one of the Montreal newspapers, in an article dealing with this subject, the opinion that some arrangement must be made looking to the settlement of our railway problem. We have thousands of miles of unnecessary lines of two great systems competing with each other, adding tremendously to overhead costs, and we have competition in telegraph and express services as well. Then, again, there are hundreds of unnecessary stations scattered throughout the country in places where one station would better serve the purpose than two.
Unless parliament deals with this question the people of Canada will deal with the men whom they have sent here and who are sidestepping the issue; for this is going to be the issue in this country from now on. There is altogether too much partyism in Canada in connection with our railway problem and the people themselves will insist upon their representatives coming to parliament with a determination to find some satisfactory solution for it. Only this morning I was talking

with a young man of about thirty-five who said while the young men in his community were not quite conscious of. what was wrong with Canada they were determined, so far as lay in their power, to get rid of party politics. He said, "Unless you old timers do something we will find new and younger men who will undertake to solve this problem, among others." I repeat, we are simply sidestepping this issue to-day as we have been doing all along. The presentation of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) this afternoon offers no solution. I thought that he would introduce some new proposal in which there might be some ray of hope. I have not of course had time to study the statement he has made, and while there may be some promise in it, I do not think that the minister has really touched the problem. The duplication in headquarters staffs and in various branches of the railway service still exists. We have engaged on the railways of Canada 30.000 or 40,000 men with whom we could dispense. If we consolidated the two systems we could pay these men $1,000 each a year until they were able to find other occupations and still we should save hundreds of millions of dollars. We are simply wasting money to-day, and we shall continue to waste money until we tackle the problem in real earnest. Neither the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) nor his government has taken hold of it, and I regret to say that the opposition offers no real constructive policy. Some people tell us that time will settle the question. Yes, time will settle it. Time will settle the politicians who refuse to deal satisfactorily with it. I have gone up and down this country and have been sick at heart to see the rivalry between our two railways. We have duplicate trains running between Toronto and Montreal and Toronto and Ottawa, and the same thing is true throughout the country. We know that the Canadian National Railways to-day have 70 per cent of the railway strategy in Canada, while the Canadian Pacific Railway has an equal advantage in regard to steamship lines. The president of that system I was reading to-day, is going to England on a mission in connection with this service, and I take this to be an indication that the Canadian Pacific is getting ready for some form of co-operation or consolidation.
We must remember that transportation is not confined to the railways alone; in its broadest sense it includes water service and motor and bus transportation. The passenger business on our railways is declining. Yesterday I was at Niagara, one of the most

CJ\.R.-Minister's Statement
glorious parts of the country, and I saw vast numbers of automobiles-an evidence of the falling off in railway passenger service.
Another formidable competition which our railways have to face is water transportation. As soon as the St. Lawrence waterways are completed, perhaps with the completion of the Georgian Bay canal, we shall see ocean ports on the Great Lakes, up to Duluth, Fort AVilliam and Port Arthur, and the competition which will ensue will be a very serious matter indeed for our railways. It will then be imperative for them to eliminate unnecessary competition to the utmost, if they are to pay half their costs.
It is regrettable that the government has not the courage to propound a policy looking in the direction of co-operation and consolidation. If they would only make overtures towards that end I hiave no doubt that the Canadian Pacific would lend a sympathetic ear. The government should make some step in this direction; otherwise the country will express its opinion in no mistak-able terms. [DOT]	.
To-day for the first time the new Minister of Railways has addressed the House as a meeting of shareholders. I am here to-day as a shareholder in this railway representing
50,000	citizens of Canada, and some hon. -gentlemen represent even a greater number. Well, I do not know how I am going to face my electors and explain to them why this unnecessary, this unwise, this scandalous competition between our two great railway systems is allowed to continue. We cannot keep it up. The government are going to bring down the rate structure, and they are going to tell the people of the west, who are greatly concerned in freight rates, that they will be able to give them lower rates. But I say you cannot have lower freight rates in this country while this unnecessary competition is allowed to continue. You can reduce the freight rates only by consolidating your two great transportation systems covering water transportation and transportation by rail. By such a consolidation we will reduce operating and other expenses, and it is only by this economy of operation and management that you can give what the Canadian farmer is calling for-lower freight rates. There must be a merging of these two railways with their steamship services. We must also provide for airway transportation and link it up with this consolidation.
I wonder if hon. members have any conception of the high-class service that the United States government is maintaining for the transfer of money and mails in that great MOl 1-235
country. It is a splendid service, and I am told that saving in interest alone by rapid transfer of money pays the cost of operation. We must be prepared to inaugurate a similar service in conjunction with a fconsolidated railway and steamboat service. We cannot afford to sidestep the issue any longer. The present unnecessary duplication is costing this country an annual waste of about 1300,000,000. This is not efficiency. One of the greatest improvements possible under a consolidation such as I have urged will be improved re-routing of all traffic. Any traffic man will tell you what a great saving and what a great improvement in service this will bring about. There is something in the suggestion of bringing about a new capital structure, but that is not the way to achieve the purpose we have in view. The people of this country, especially the western people, want lower freight rates, and they are not going to get them unless we consolidate our transportation facilities. We must stop spending more money in trying to run these two great railway systems; we must consolidate them. That is the keynote of the situation. I am glad to that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is listening to me. He must know that it will be a problem for him to go to the people and say:	I am still a
party to this mad competition in railway service. He cannot face his electors, nor do I believe that half of us in this House can face our electors and justify that mad business. Go where I will I find the people are responding to what I have said in this House with regard to this vital question. They are glad to see me, and they are even beginning to ask me to address meetings on the subject. While I have been scarified in some quarters because I had the courage to say the other night that this House ought to appoint a committee to deal with the question, and that once an agreement was made between the whips of the respective parties it ought to be carried out, while I was said to be a "bad Conservative" for having so expressed myself, yet I am content to disregard those attacks and to go on the platform and justifiy my action. I am not going to talk on any minor issues if there is an appeal to the country-and I warn the House again that there is every prospect of a general election in a very short time.

No, I am not
wrong, my brother; perhaps you are looking the wrong way. I am confident that something is likely to force the government

CJtf.R.-Minister's Statement

to go to the country, and then this and other problems will have to be presented to the electorate, and we shall have to defend or condemn this mad rivalry we are now maintaining between express companies, telegraph companies and railway companies. By a consolidation of our great transportation systems we would get much greater efficiency and we would get real service both by rail and by water, and we would be also prepared for that formidable competition which our railway systems will have to meet as soon as the St. Lawrence route has 'been deepened to allow ocean-going vessels to reach Port Arthur and Duluth. With the competition from that quarter and from motor transport there will be no future for two competing railways in this country. In fact even to-day there is only room for one consolidated system which will include transportation by water and transportation by rail. This, as I say, will permit of better routing of the roads, and in this will be found the real salvation of Canada's transportation needs, rather than in a reduction of freight rates. Stop this mad competition, start re-routing your lines, and you will see a great improvement in the railway service of this country. The Minister of Railways has told us about establishing a new capital Structure for the Canadian National Railways, but I tell him we have got to have a new capital structure of all our commitments in connection both with the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. When that is brought about it will be easy to create a system of transportation which, while giving the people what they desire, will stop the extravagance which prevails all over the country to-day.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with other members on this side of the House I listened with a great deal of pleasure and attention to the instructive address of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) this afternoon. I congratulate him upon having presented his case in a very lucid manner. He has the advantage, of course, of the expert advice and assistance of the officials of the Canadian National Railways, and also of their expert accountants. It would be somewhat more satisfactory to the House, I think, if from time to time those who are in actual control of the Canadian

National Railways should appear before hon. members in committee in order that a clearer understanding might be had of some of the points which are beclouded by the public discussions of the day. I have not had the assistance such as the Minister of Railways has had, but a few salient facts are before me which I should like to present for the consideration of the House.
I will not go back to 1867, when the construction of the Intercolonial was undertaken at the expense of the government, or to the time when the Prince Edward Island railway was commenced. However, in order that we may ascertain the present financial obligations of the country with regard to railways I should like to present a few statistics running back to the year 1903, when the government undertook the construction of the eastern division of the National Transcontinental line from Moncton to Winnipeg, on the understanding that it was to be taken over by the Grand Trunk Pacific under lease and operated in connection with the western section of that road. In 1914 further obligations were assumed by the government of the country when the Canadian Northern Railway Company began to collapse, and large loans or advances were necessary in order to keep that road in operation at the outbreak of the war. In 1917 further obligations were undertaken when the Canadian Northern railway lines were taken over by the government. Going -back for two years before that, on the failure of the -Grand Trunk Pacific to operate the eastern section of its road the government was compelled to include the eastern section of the Transcontinental railway in its railway system. In 1916 I find that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway began to ask the Dominion government for loans and advances; and finally, in 1918, the government was compelled to take over that line and assume its obligations. In 1919, I think it was, the Grand Trunk railway was taken over, and since that time has been operated as part of the Canadian National system. I have had a schedule prepared. It is not very lengthy but it shows from year to year since 1903 the increasing mileage of the National Railway system. Then the second column shows the total long term indebtedness of that system, being the amount of money expended by the Dominion government, together with securities bought and held by the people of Canada, and other countries, for all of which the government is really liable. In the third column there is shown the increase of government liability from year to year, which is represented by the difference between

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
the total expenditures made upon the system and the total received from operation. The .fourth column gives the annual fixed charges, being the annual fixed interest charge which the Canadian government will have to pay to the holders of Canadian National Railway securities and Dominion government securities issued to raise loans made by the government to the Canadian National system. This is to be paid for all time or until the securities are redeemed by the income of the government realized from taxation of the people of Canada. This statement shows, as the Minister of Finance stated, that on December 31, 1925, there was a total long term indebtedness, which was an indebtedness primarily of the Canadian National Railway but equally an indebtedness of the Canadian government and the Canadian people, amounting to $2,119,811,644. I have excluded the amounts owing on ordinary revenue accounts of the year. I have simply taken the long term obligations of the Canadian people in this respect, and I find that this annual increase in capital liability has been continued from year to year. When we took over the liabilities of
14011-235i
the Canadian Northern in September, 1918, there was an increase in liability made up from that source and others of $730,000,000. It was $580,000,000 in 1920 and $132,000,000 in 1921.
Is my hon. friend right in saying that we took over the liability of the Canadian Northern in 1918? Was it not the Grand Trunk?
I said the Canadian government assumed the liability of the Canadian Northern in 1918.
Is my hon. friend correct in that?
There may be some mistake about it.
Was it not the Grand Trunk?

The government became
the receiver of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway system in March 1919 and assumed control of the Grand Trunk Railway in May 1920. I have taken from year to year, with the assistance of an expert accountant, the annual increase in liability since that date down to December 31, 1925. There were increases in liabilities as follows:

And in 1925 I find an increase of long term obligations of $63,630,000, Naturally with this large increase in capital obligations the annual fixed charges of the Canadian National Railway have increased from year to year. In 1919 I find that the annual fixed charges for interest amounted in round figures to $29,000,000. In 1925 I find that they amounted to $71,888,000, showing that the railway loans had been extended, and as their obligations had increased it resulted in a large annual increase in the fixed charges payable by the Canadian National Railway lines in respect of those capital obligations.

Will my hon. friend tell me whether that $63,000,000 increase which he speaks of for 1925 does not include the amount due the government for interest, $31,000,000? That I presume is true of all the other years.

Certainly that is so, and that is an obligation, is it not? I do not agree with the hon. member's suggestion that when the government advances money to the railway from time to time the interest accruing to the government is not an obligation of the National lines; and if.'it is not paid of course it is an increase in the obligations

CJV.fi.-Minister's Statement
of the National lines for which the people of this country are directly and indirectly responsible. As I progress I will make that perfectly plain. Dealing with the question of interest, I noticed a statement of Mr. J. L. Payne in the London Free Press in July last, in which this matter is discussed pro and con. He deals with the fixed charges for the year 1924, and I think there is a great deal to be said for the contention he makes in the Free Press. He says:
How much are those fixed charges? The official announcement placed them at $69,632,747, but beyond the possibility of doubt that is not the correct amount.
He is dealing with 1924. The statement continues:
It is merely the sum set down against the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk; and in these cases it does not allow for unpaid interests on a compound basis, as standard accounting would require. Interest charges on the capital liability of the Intercolonial, the Prince Edward Island, the Quebec bridge, and all eastern branch lines, representing at least $1,000,000,000 are omitted. The excuse, certainly not the defence, for such irregular accounting, is that such liability is incorporated with the National debt. That is true, but it also very distinctly and properly is a part of the railway account. If it were brought into the railway statement, as it should be, fixed charges would reach a total of considerably more than $100,000,000 per annum.
The statement is frequently made in respect to the extension of colonization roads that these roads simply pass the interest upon the amount expended upon them during their construction. In the case of a private company or a privately owned utility company there is an additional cost to the aggregate cost of construction, a cost resulting from the interest charges on the amount expended in the construction until the road is in a condition, if it is a private utility, to pay its operating costs and its fixed charges. That is as much a cost on capital account in respect of the road as money actually expended on construction. According to the report of Mr. G. A. Bell, Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, which is now published and circulated as a government return, I find that the long-term funded indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways amounted on December 31, 1924, to $2,056,181,516 and on December 31, 1925, it had increased to $2,119,811,644. That is how I ascertained my increase for the year 1925, the difference showing the increase in liabilities of $63,630,128 as I stated.
I cal this long term liability because I am not dealing with any amounts owing on current account or petty banking accounts or for materials bought in for the operation of the road. I am leaving this out of account and

this amount, of $2,119,811,644 would, I think, be somewhat increased if I took into account these other smaller amounts which are changing from month to month during the year's operations.
Of this amount the security held by the public amounted to $931,329,303. Loans from the Dominion government made directly to these companies, not including the old loans made with respect to the Grand Trunk railway t.o which the Minister of Finance referred, but loans recently made within the term with which I am dealing, amounted in actual cash to $572,685,535. That does not include interest on Dominion government loans or the appropriation account of the Canadian government railways.
